PaperManager is open source and grows with other people's pull requests. Thank you to Antoine Luciano for researcher CVs, the duplicate-people finder and surname order on the People page (#36, People guide).

docs.title: Add a paper
docs.text: Drag in a PDF or paste an arXiv, DOI or PubMed link. The metadata is looked up for you; you check it and press save.

docs.title: PaperManager reads it
docs.text: In the background it writes a summary, pulls out figures, tables and references, and suggests topics and tags.

docs.title: You read, ask and connect
docs.text: Read the PDF with the summary, a guided tour and visual explanations beside it, then ask questions across everything you have read.

docs.title: One library for every paper
docs.text:
Search titles, authors, your notes and highlights and the full text in one box, ranked, with every hit showing why it matched; filter by project, topic, tag, author or reading status, and see at a glance what is still unread.

Library

docs.title: A profile for every author
docs.text:
Each researcher gets a CV built from OpenAlex, ORCID, Wikidata and their homepage, checked against the papers in your library so a namesake is not mistaken for them. People listed under several spellings are found and merged in one click. Contributed by Antoine Luciano.

People

docs.title: Everything about a paper in one view
docs.text:
The left side switches between the PDF, the summary, figures, tables, references and related papers. The right side keeps your notes, highlights and a chat about the paper open beside it.

Reading a paper

docs.title: A guided tour through a long paper
docs.text:
An overview, what you can skip, and 6–12 stops that jump to the passages that matter, with the concepts each one relies on.

Concepts, tour and concept map

docs.title: How a whole project fits together
docs.text:
The key concepts of every paper in a project and how they relate, as a graph you can filter by author, year and kind of concept.

Concept map

docs.title: Ask your whole library
docs.text:
The knowledge chat answers from your papers and cites them; a citation opens the paper beside the chat. Answers can carry concept cards (formulas, plots, animations) and 3D protein structures you can rotate. Narrow a question with @project:, @topic: or @paper:, branch off from any question, or let it search the web too.

Knowledge chat

docs.title: Who publishes what at NeurIPS, ICML, CVPR, ACL, ...
docs.text:
Browse the accepted papers of 22 conference series by institution (rank, research-area mix, collaborators, every paper) or by topic: type one or paste an abstract and see which universities and companies publish most on it and the closest papers, one click from your library. One search box covers all loaded conferences at once: papers, authors, and where a topic is published, per conference and over the years.

Conference explorer

docs.title: Under the hood
docs.text:
graph LR
    UI["React app"] --> API["FastAPI backend"]
    MCP["Claude via MCP"] --> API
    API --> DB[("Neo4j<br/>knowledge graph")]
    API --> Drive["Google Drive<br/>PDFs and figures"]
    API --> LLM["Claude / any<br/>OpenAI-compatible model"]
    API --> Ext["Semantic Scholar<br/>CrossRef · arXiv"]

Every paper, author, topic, project, note and concept is a node in one Neo4j graph, so the same data powers the library, the chat, the concept map and the Cypher editor. PDFs stay in your own Google Drive. More in Architecture.

PaperManager is open source. The project page at niklas-abraham.de has the story behind it; issues and pull requests are welcome on GitHub.

docs.title: Set up with your coding agent
docs.text:
The quickest way to your own PaperManager is to let a coding agent install it. This works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other agents that can run commands on your computer. Open one in any folder and say:

Set up PaperManager for me by following https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager/blob/main/DEPLOY.md

DEPLOY.md is a runbook written for the agent. It tells the agent to:

  1. Check your machine. Git and Docker must be present and Docker must be running. If something is missing, the agent explains how to install it and asks before installing.
  2. Ask you a few questions, one at a time:
    • your login name
    • which AI account you have: Anthropic, OpenAI, both, or your own OpenAI-compatible server
    • where to keep PDFs: on this computer (default) or in Google Drive
    • an accent colour for the app
  3. Write .env. The agent generates the database password and session secret itself. You paste your API key into the file yourself, so it never passes through the chat.
  4. Build and start the app with Docker. The first build takes about 10 minutes.
  5. Hand you one command to set your password in your own terminal.
  6. Run scripts/check_setup.py. It checks the database, the AI provider (with one tiny test message) and the file storage, then shows the address to open.

docs.title: What your answers change
docs.text:
Every answer is stored in .env, and the app reads it at startup:

Answer Setting Effect Anthropic key ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Summaries, topics, claims and the concept map run on Claude Haiku 4.5. Chat and concept visualisations use Claude Sonnet/Opus OpenAI key OPENAI_API_KEY Summaries and chat run on GPT-5 mini Own server LITELLM_ENDPOINT, LITELLM_MODEL Any OpenAI-compatible API (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM) runs the fast tasks PDFs on this computer STORAGE_BACKEND=local Files go into the Docker volume paper_files. No Google account needed PDFs in Drive STORAGE_BACKEND=drive Files go to a Google Drive folder (setup) Accent colour UI_ACCENT Buttons, links and highlights use your colour (a preset name or any #RRGGBB)

AI_PROVIDER=auto uses the first configured provider in this order: your own server, then Anthropic, then OpenAI. Set AI_PROVIDER or FAST_MODEL to override that choice. If your own server fails and an Anthropic key is set, the fast tasks retry on Claude Haiku (AI_FALLBACK=false turns that off). The model menus in the app show the active model by name, and Claude options appear only for users who have a Claude key.

To change something later, edit .env and run docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d. A colour or model change needs no rebuild.

docs.title: Without an agent
docs.text: Every step in DEPLOY.md is a plain shell command, so you can follow it yourself. The hosting guide covers Heroku, servers and Google Drive in detail.

docs.title: DB: Neo4j Aura (cloud) over SQLite
docs.text: Papers, people, topics, and tags are naturally a graph. Enables path queries, co-authorship derivation, topic clustering. Free tier (200k nodes / 400k relationships) sufficient for personal use.

docs.title: Tags as nodes, not property arrays
docs.text: Tags are first-class citizens for filtering and browsing. (Paper)-[:TAGGED]->(Tag) lets you query "all papers with this tag" efficiently.

docs.title: Topic ≠ Tag
docs.text:
• Topic = formal research area, linked to Person specialties
  • Tag = free-form personal label (source, status, context, anything)

docs.title: Notes as separate nodes
docs.text: Notes need their own @mention and #topic relationships. A text field on Paper would lose this graph power.

docs.title: INVOLVES relationship with role property
docs.text: Instead of many typed relationships for workflow states, one INVOLVES {role} relationship keeps the schema flexible. New roles can be invented freely without schema changes.

docs.title: Metadata extraction: four-layer chain
docs.text:
1. DOI regex → Semantic Scholar API (preferred) or CrossRef (fallback) — covers ~80–90% of papers
  2. Ollama + llama3.2:3b local LLM — for papers without DOI (drafts, internal reports)
  3. Regex heuristics — last resort, user corrects in UI
  4. Abstract fallback: ABSTRACT_RE regex → Claude Haiku

metadata_source field on Paper node records which layer was used. Semantic Scholar also returns topics + citation count → auto-populates Topic nodes.

docs.title: MCP server shares the same service layer as FastAPI
docs.text: db/queries/ and services/ are framework-neutral. FastAPI routers/ and MCP tools/ are two thin entry-point layers over the same logic. Every capability is available both via HTTP and via Claude Desktop tool calls. PDF upload is intentionally not exposed as an MCP tool — file upload via browser only.

docs.title: No Collection node (for now)
docs.text: Projects serve a similar purpose and are already in scope. Can revisit if the need for lightweight grouping (reading lists) emerges.

docs.title: Backend: FastAPI
docs.text: Python-native, strong async support, automatic OpenAPI docs.

docs.title: Frontend: React + Vite + Tailwind
docs.text: Standard modern SPA stack; fast HMR during development.

docs.title: Knowledge Chat: agentic tool-use over hybrid retrieval
docs.text: Instead of stuffing all paper text into context, the backend pre-loads a relevance-ranked subset and gives Claude two tools: run_cypher (live graph queries) and semantic_search (vector similarity). Claude decides what additional data it needs. This keeps context manageable while allowing Claude to chase any lead in the graph.

docs.title: Vector embeddings on Paper nodes
docs.text: 768-dim Ollama nomic-embed-text embeddings stored directly on Paper.embedding. A Neo4j vector index (paper_embeddings) enables ANN cosine search at query time. Chosen over a separate vector store (Pinecone, etc.) to keep the stack minimal.

docs.title: Hybrid retrieval: vector + recency fallback
docs.text: Vector search alone fails when embeddings haven't been generated yet (cold start). The recency fallback (10 most recently added papers) ensures Knowledge Chat is useful from day one without a backfill step.

docs.title: Conversation compaction with structured working memory
docs.text: Simple truncation loses context. Claude Haiku extracts a JSON block of key findings, open questions, and decisions before compaction. Specific numbers and paper titles survive in the structured JSON even after the messages are replaced.

docs.title: Claims as graph nodes
docs.text: Claim extraction enables evidence-level queries via Cypher. Claims are NOT injected into Knowledge Chat context by default (would bloat it); Claude pulls them on demand via run_cypher when it needs evidence-level detail.

docs.title: Chapters for books and lecture decks
docs.text: document_type on Paper controls the upload pipeline. Books and lecture decks skip summary/figures/references/claims but support chapters. Chapters are detected in three passes: Docling structural → regex → Ollama AI.

docs.title: Blogs as first-class nodes
docs.text: Technical blog posts (Distill, Lil'Log, etc.) are valuable context alongside papers. Blog (feed) and BlogPost (individual post) nodes allow the same tag/project/chat workflows used for papers to apply to blog content.

docs.title: Annotations (PDF highlights) stored in Neo4j
docs.text: Highlights stored as Annotation nodes linked to Paper, not as PDF metadata. This keeps annotations queryable and database-portable.

docs.title: Author tracking with Semantic Scholar
docs.text: Person.tracked = true + Person.s2_author_id enables automatic import of new papers. S2 is queried periodically; new papers are ingested just like URL ingest.

docs.title: JWT authentication with admin-managed users
docs.text: Single-user primary focus, but multi-user support needed for collaboration. JWT stored in localStorage; admin user manages create/update/delete. Admin capabilities restricted to username niklas in current implementation.

docs.title: Rate limiting as in-process middleware
docs.text: Sliding-window rate limiter in services/rate_limit.py (no Redis dependency). Stricter limits on /auth/login to prevent brute-force attacks.

docs.title: Docker Compose + Traefik for production
docs.text: Three services: Neo4j, FastAPI backend, Nginx-served React frontend. Traefik handles SSL (Let's Encrypt) and routing. Neo4j and backend are internal-only; only the Nginx container is internet-facing.

docs.title: Conference data on disk, not in Neo4j
docs.text: A conference is 3,000–9,000 papers and as many people; as Paper and Person nodes they would swamp the library, the duplicate scanner and the free-tier node limit. Each conference-year is a JSON file plus a float16 embedding matrix under /data/conferences; only "+ Library" writes to the graph.

docs.title: Official miniconf feeds first, Paper Copilot for the rest
docs.text: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR, ICCV and ECCV publish every accepted paper with each author's institution as one JSON file, so no scraping and no OpenReview profile crawl (OpenReview's API refuses anonymous clients). Paper Copilot's lists cover the other venues and older years.

docs.title: bge-small on CPU through transformers, no new dependency
docs.text: transformers and torch are already installed for Docling. bge-small-en-v1.5 (33 M parameters) embeds a 6,500-paper conference in two minutes from titles, or 3,000–6,000 papers with abstracts in 7–15 minutes, on four CPU threads, in the background, and needs no API key, so the feature works in the default self-hosted setup.

docs.title: One area taxonomy for every conference, assigned zero-shot
docs.text: 24 hand-described areas instead of per-conference clustering: the same area has the same name and colour at every venue, so conferences can be compared. Embeddings are centred on the conference mean before assignment; without it the most generic area absorbed a fifth of NeurIPS.

docs.title: One ranked search over every source, scored in Python
docs.text: The old /search passed the raw query to two Lucene indexes (titles/abstracts/summaries and notes), crashed on : or -, and could not find a paper by author, DOI, highlight or full text. Now each source (paper fields, author/topic/tag names, venue, notes, highlights, claims, full text, DOI/arXiv id) gets its own Lucene query, and the per-paper merge, coverage check and scoring happen in Python (services/library_search/). Lucene scores are not comparable across indexes, so each source is normalised by its best score and weighted; title and author bonuses come from the title and names themselves. Pure functions, so the ranking is unit-tested without Neo4j, and the MCP library_search tool uses the same engine.

docs.title: Every word must match somewhere, relaxed only when nothing does
docs.text: Lucene's default OR returned any paper with any word ("antibody docking" → every antibody paper). A hit must now cover every query word across its fields (author + title counts); only when no paper does are partial matches shown, flagged relaxed.

docs.title: standard-folding analyzer, indexes rebuilt at startup
docs.text: Case and accents must not matter (Kynkaanniemi = Kynkäänniemi). The search indexes moved to Neo4j's standard-folding analyzer and the query terms are folded the same way in Python (prefix and fuzzy terms bypass Lucene's analyzer). db/schema.py drops and rebuilds an index whose analyzer differs: seconds on this library, and simpler than versioned index names.

docs.title: Full text in Lucene, not CONTAINS
docs.text: The MCP tool scanned toLower(p.raw_text) CONTAINS over every paper: 220–270 ms per query on 36 MB of text. A full-text index on raw_text (eventually consistent, so uploads do not wait) costs 13 MB and answers in single-digit milliseconds.

docs.title: Hybrid by reciprocal-rank fusion, semantic weight scaled by confidence
docs.text: Library embeddings reuse the conference explorer's bge-small (no new dependency), stored in a file like the conference vectors, synced incrementally by a background thread. Semantic and lexical lists are fused by weighted RRF; the semantic weight shrinks when even the best cosine is low (jargon the model does not know), the lexical weight when the query is a long question.

docs.title: Library citations as a prior
docs.text: Among many papers matching "flow matching", the one most cited by the library's own papers is almost always the one meant. Scores are multiplied by 1 + 0.12 ln(1 + citing papers).

docs.title: Hosting your own PaperManager
docs.text:
Easiest: let your coding agent do it

Tell Claude Code, Codex or another coding agent: "Set up PaperManager for me by following https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager/blob/main/DEPLOY.md". It asks a few questions and runs the local setup below for you. See Set up with your agent.

This guide sets up your own instance with your own database and your own keys. You can run it on your own computer (localhost) or on Heroku. Both use the same container image, Dockerfile.selfhost. It holds the React frontend, served by nginx, and the FastAPI backend, and serves both from one port. The login cookie only works when the page and the API come from the same origin, so they share that port.

docker-compose.example.yml mirrors the maintainer's production stack (Traefik, his domain, a remote GPU machine). Don't use it. Use docker-compose.selfhost.yml or heroku.yml.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
Thing Required? Used for Git and Docker (Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows) yes building and running the app An Anthropic API key (console.anthropic.com) or an OpenAI API key (platform.openai.com) one of them summaries, topics, chat. With Anthropic the fast tasks run on Claude Haiku 4.5; with OpenAI everything runs on GPT-5 mini A Google account plus a Google Cloud project only for Drive storage, and always on Heroku PDFs in Google Drive. Locally, STORAGE_BACKEND=local keeps them in a Docker volume An OpenAI-compatible endpoint (LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Ollama) optional runs the fast tasks on your own model A Heroku account plus the Heroku CLI only for Heroku hosting A Neo4j AuraDB Free instance (console.neo4j.io) only for Heroku the database (locally, Docker runs Neo4j for you)

Expect around 2 GB of RAM for the app container. The PDF layout model (Docling) runs inside it and loads PyTorch.

docs.title: Step 1: get the code and create .env
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager.git
cd PaperManager
cp .env.example .env

Edit .env. Keep it private, since it is your secrets file and is git-ignored. Change these values and leave everything else at its default:

NEO4J_PASSWORD=<any long random string>        # locally: Docker creates the DB with this password
JWT_SECRET_KEY=<output of: openssl rand -hex 32>
DEFAULT_USER_NAME=<your login name>             # the owner/admin account
DEFAULT_USER_PASSWORD=                          # leave empty; you set it in step 4
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...                    # or OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
STORAGE_BACKEND=local                           # or drive, with GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID from step 2
UI_ACCENT=violet                                # or blue, teal, green, amber, rose, slate, #RRGGBB

# The maintainer's private infrastructure: switch it off
DOCLING_MODE=local
INFERENCE_MANAGER_URL=
HERMIONE_HOST=
LITELLM_ENDPOINT=
LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL=

Keep comments on their own line in the real file: Docker reads KEY= # note as the value # note. The comments above are only there to explain each line.

For your own model on the fast tasks, point LiteLLM at any OpenAI-compatible API, for example LITELLM_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, LITELLM_API_KEY=<openrouter key>, LITELLM_MODEL=google/gemma-3-27b-it.

Leave CLAUDE_CODE_USERS and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN empty. That feature runs chats on the server owner's personal Claude subscription, and only the owner may use it. If you have your own Claude Pro/Max plan and want it for yourself, set CLAUDE_CODE_USERS=<your login name>. Then put the output of claude setup-token (from Claude Code) into CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN. Never list other people there.

docs.title: Step 2: Google Drive access (once, on your own computer)
docs.text:
Skip this step locally with STORAGE_BACKEND=local. On Heroku it is required, because Heroku has no disk to keep files on. For Drive locally, also uncomment the two credentials.json / token.json lines in docker-compose.selfhost.yml.

  1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and create a project. Open APIs & Services → Library, then enable the Google Drive API.
  2. Open APIs & Services → OAuth consent screen. Choose user type External, fill in the app name and your e-mail, and add yourself as a test user.
  3. Open APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → OAuth client ID, with application type Desktop app. Download the JSON and save it as backend/credentials.json.
  4. In Google Drive, create a folder for the PDFs. Its ID is the last part of the folder URL (https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/<THIS>). Put it into GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID.
  5. Create the login token. A browser window opens; log in and allow access:
python3 -m venv .venv-drive
.venv-drive/bin/pip install google-auth-oauthlib google-api-python-client
.venv-drive/bin/python backend/scripts/setup_drive_oauth.py

This writes backend/token.json. Both credentials.json and token.json are git-ignored. Never commit them.

docs.title: Step 3a: run on localhost
docs.text:
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml up -d --build   # first build takes ~10 min
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml logs -f app      # wait for "Application startup complete"

Create your account (step 4), then open http://localhost:8080.

  • Stop: docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml down. Your data stays in the neo4j_data volume. down -v deletes it.
  • Update: git pull, then run the up -d --build command again.

docs.title: Step 3b: run on Heroku
docs.text:
Heroku has no free tier and no persistent disk, so the database lives on Neo4j AuraDB Free.

  1. Create an AuraDB Free instance at console.neo4j.io. Save the generated password. Note the connection URI (neo4j+s://xxxx.databases.neo4j.io).
  2. Create the app and switch it to container builds:
heroku login
heroku create <app-name>                  # e.g. papers-alex → https://papers-alex-xxxx.herokuapp.com
heroku stack:set container -a <app-name>
  1. Set the configuration. Use the same values as in .env, plus the Heroku-specific ones:
APP_HOST=<app-name>-xxxx.herokuapp.com    # the host from `heroku apps:info -a <app-name>`
heroku config:set -a <app-name> \
  NEO4J_URI='neo4j+s://xxxx.databases.neo4j.io' NEO4J_USER=neo4j NEO4J_PASSWORD='<aura password>' \
  JWT_SECRET_KEY="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" DEFAULT_USER_NAME='<your login name>' \
  ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='sk-ant-...' \
  GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID='<folder id>' \
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID='<client_id from credentials.json>' \
  GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET='<client_secret from credentials.json>' \
  GOOGLE_TOKEN_JSON="$(cat backend/token.json)" \
  DOCLING_MODE=local INFERENCE_MANAGER_URL= HERMIONE_HOST= LITELLM_ENDPOINT= LITELLM_EMBED_MODEL= \
  FRONTEND_URL="https://$APP_HOST" TRUSTED_HOSTS="$APP_HOST" TRUST_PROXY_HEADERS=true

Heroku has no disk to keep token.json on, so GOOGLE_TOKEN_JSON passes its contents as a variable. GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET are inside backend/credentials.json.

  1. Deploy. heroku.yml makes Heroku build Dockerfile.selfhost:
git push heroku main
heroku ps:type web=standard-2x -a <app-name>   # 1 GB RAM; basic (512 MB) runs out of memory
heroku logs --tail -a <app-name>               # wait for "Application startup complete"

If a PDF upload crashes with "Memory quota exceeded" in the logs, the layout model needs more memory. Use performance-m. Heroku also cuts every request off after 30 seconds (error H12). Long PDFs can take longer than that to process, so very large uploads may fail on Heroku even though they work locally.

  1. Create your account (step 4), then open https://<APP_HOST>.

To update: git pull from GitHub, then git push heroku main again.

docs.title: Step 4: create your account
docs.text:
The account named DEFAULT_USER_NAME is the owner and admin. It is also the only account that uses the server-wide ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. Other users you add later enter their own key under Settings.

# localhost
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml exec app python scripts/create_default_user.py
# Heroku
heroku run -a <app-name> python scripts/create_default_user.py

The script asks for a password (at least 8 characters).

Log in, then follow First steps to add your first paper and try the tour, the concept map and the chat.

docs.title: PaperManager — UI Style Guide

docs.title: AI Pipelines
docs.text: PaperManager uses multiple AI models for different tasks. This page documents each pipeline, the models used, and how they fit together.

docs.title: Models Used
docs.text:
Model Provider Used for claude-opus-4-6 Anthropic Paper summarisation, single-paper chat, knowledge chat, cross-paper synthesis, research gap analysis claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 Anthropic Abstract extraction, reference extraction, topic suggestion, claim extraction, chapter summarisation, conversation compaction, figure captioning (claude-vision mode) llama3.2:3b Ollama (local) Metadata extraction (layer 2), tag suggestion, chapter detection, figure captions (default), affiliation extraction, Cypher assist, merge scan nomic-embed-text Ollama (local) Paper embedding vectors for semantic similarity search

All Anthropic calls can be routed through an enterprise Foundry gateway by setting ANTHROPIC_WORK_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_WORK_BASE_URL.

docs.title: Metadata Extraction Pipeline (PDF Upload)
docs.text:
Runs when a PDF is uploaded. Tries strategies in order, stopping at the first success:

flowchart TD
    Start["PDF bytes"] --> Extract["Docling extracts raw_text"]
    Extract --> FindDOI{DOI / arXiv ID\nfound in text?}

    FindDOI -->|"Yes"| S2["Layer 1a: Semantic Scholar API"]
    S2 -->|fail| CR["Layer 1a fallback: CrossRef API"]

    FindDOI -->|"No DOI but\ntitle found"| S2Title["Layer 1b: S2 title search"]

    FindDOI -->|"Nothing found"| Ollama["Layer 2: Ollama llama3.2:3b\non first 3 000 chars"]
    Ollama -->|"Ollama unavailable"| Heuristic["Layer 3: Regex heuristics\n(first line = title, year regex)"]

    S2 --> AbstractCheck{Abstract\nextracted?}
    CR --> AbstractCheck
    S2Title --> AbstractCheck
    Ollama --> AbstractCheck
    Heuristic --> AbstractCheck

    AbstractCheck -->|"No"| AbstractFallback["ABSTRACT_RE regex\n→ Claude Haiku if regex fails"]
    AbstractCheck -->|"Yes"| Done["Metadata ready"]
    AbstractFallback --> Done
Layer Trigger Service Output 1a (primary) DOI or arXiv ID in text Semantic Scholar API title, year, authors, abstract, topics, citation count, venue 1a (fallback) S2 fails CrossRef API title, year, authors, doi, venue 1b Title found, no DOI S2 title search same as 1a 2 No DOI, no useful title Ollama llama3.2:3b on raw_text[:3000] title, year, authors (structured JSON) 3 Ollama unavailable Regex on raw_text title (first non-empty line), year (4-digit year regex) Abstract fallback Abstract still missing ABSTRACT_RE regex → Claude Haiku abstract text

The metadata_source property on the Paper node records which layer was used.

docs.text:
Triggered after PDF upload or via POST /backfill/summary / POST /{id}/regenerate-summary.

flowchart LR
    A["abstract + raw_text"] --> P["Load prompts/summary.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Opus 4.6"]
    C --> S["summary string\nsaved to Paper.summary"]

The prompt at prompts/summary.txt structures output as: Problem / motivation · Key method or contribution · Main findings · Relevance.

docs.text:
Triggered during upload, via POST /papers/{id}/topics/suggest, or bulk backfill.

flowchart LR
    A["title + abstract"] --> P["Load prompts/topics.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Haiku"]
    C --> T["3–6 title-case topic strings"]
    T --> DB["MERGE Topic nodes\n+ ABOUT relationships"]

docs.text:

docs.title: Reference Extraction Pipeline
docs.text:
Triggered via GET /papers/{id}/extract-references or POST /papers/{id}/references.

flowchart TD
    Start["Paper with raw_text"] --> P["Parser over every reference section\n(count = yardstick)"]
    P --> A{DOI / arXiv id?}
    A -->|"Yes"| S2["A: Semantic Scholar /references"]
    S2 -->|"≥ 80% of parser count"| Done["Reference list"]
    S2 -->|"short or none"| LLM["B: LLM over the section\n6k-char chunks, LiteLLM then Claude"]
    A -->|"No"| LLM
    LLM -->|"≥ 80%"| Vet["Identifier check\n(citecheck: doi.org, arXiv API)"]
    LLM -->|"short"| Best["C: longest of S2 / LLM / parser"]
    Best -->|"LLM or parser"| Vet
    Best -->|"S2"| Done
    Vet --> Done

Identifier check. Before a list from the LLM or the parser is shown, every DOI and arXiv id in it is resolved (services/citecheck.py, no model): doi.org content negotiation returns the registered title, the arXiv API answers 100 ids per request, 16 lookups run in parallel within a 60 s budget. Dead ids are dropped; an id whose registered title does not match the extracted one is dropped too (LLMs invent and misremember ids, the parser can pick up the next entry's id), unless the parser's "title" is an author fragment, in which case the registered title replaces it. Each reference carries id_check. scripts/check_reference_ids.py runs the same check over existing stubs.

Each reference creates a Paper stub node tagged from-references and linked via CITES. Stubs are enriched when the full paper is later imported.

docs.title: Claim Extraction
docs.text:
Triggered automatically during upload (for papers) or via POST /papers/{id}/claims/extract.

flowchart LR
    A["raw_text + title"] --> P["Load prompts/claims.txt"]
    P --> C["Claude Haiku"]
    C --> Claims["List of {text, type} claims"]
    Claims --> DB["Create Claim nodes\nHAS_CLAIM relationships"]

Claim types include "finding", "method", "limitation", "contribution".

docs.text:

flowchart LR

    O --> V["768-dim embedding vector"]
    V --> DB["Stored on Paper.embedding\n(vector index for ANN search)"]

docs.title: Single-Paper Chat
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/chat.

docs.title: Chapter Detection (Books / Lecture Decks)
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/chapters/detect.

flowchart TD
    PDF["PDF from Google Drive"] --> Docling["Strategy 1: Docling\nstructural chapter detection"]
    Docling -->|"found chapters"| Done["Create Chapter nodes"]
    Docling -->|"no chapters"| Regex["Strategy 2: Regex\non raw_text headings"]
    Regex -->|"found chapters"| Done
    Regex -->|"no chapters"| AI["Strategy 3: Ollama AI\n(use_ai=true only)"]
    AI --> Done
    Done --> Summarize["Ollama summarizes\neach chapter"]

Each chapter node stores its text slice, title, level, page range, and summary.

Chapter chat uses prompts/chapter_chat_system.txt with Claude Haiku; chapter summary uses prompts/chapter_summary.txt with Ollama.

Triggered via POST /papers/{id}/figures/extract.

    Method -->|"ollama"| OllamaCaption["Ollama llama3.2:3b\nfrom prompts/figure_captions.txt"]
    Method -->|"claude-vision"| ClaudeCaption["Claude Haiku Vision"]
    DocCaption --> Upload["Upload PNG to Google Drive"]
    OllamaCaption --> Upload
    ClaudeCaption --> Upload
    Upload --> DB["Save Figure node in Neo4j"]

docs.title: Knowledge Chat Context Assembly
docs.text:
Triggered via POST /knowledge-chat/stream.

flowchart TD
    Q["User question"] --> Parse["Parse @mentions\n@tag:, @topic:, @project:, @paper:"]
    Parse -->|"Mentions found"| Cypher["Run Cypher queries\nto fetch matching papers"]
    Parse -->|"No mentions"| Recent["Fetch 10 most recently\nadded papers"]
    Cypher --> Budget["Apply token budget\nper paper (truncate raw_text)"]

docs.title: Affiliation Extraction

Triggered as part of paper upload when author affiliations are missing.

    C --> Results["Scored duplicate pairs\n(similarity 0–1 + reason)"]

docs.title: /search Query Parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description q string Query: words (prefix, one typo for 5+ letters), "phrases", word*, a DOI or arXiv id. Case and accents are ignored tag string Filter by tag name (case-insensitive) topic string Filter by topic name (case-insensitive) project_id string Filter by project ID person_id string Filter by person ID (authored or involved) venue string Filter by venue (case-insensitive) year_min int Minimum publication year year_max int Maximum publication year reading_status string Filter by reading status bookmarked bool Only bookmarked papers include_references bool Include reference stubs (tag from-references); default true, ranked below library papers mode string lexical (default), hybrid (lexical + embedding similarity, reciprocal-rank fusion) or semantic; falls back to lexical while the embedding index is not ready sort string relevance (default with q), date_desc (default without), date_asc, year_desc, year_asc, title_asc snippets int Passages per hit, 0–6 (default 2) skip, limit int Paging after ranking; limit 1–2000 (default 20)

Response: {results, total, mode, relaxed, semantic, failed_sources, took_ms}. total counts every hit, not just the page. Each hit is the paper plus score, matched_in (coarse, e.g. note+paper), matched_fields (doi, title, author, topic, tag, venue, abstract, summary, note, highlight, claim, fulltext, semantic), matches (matched author / topic / tag / venue names), snippets ({field, text, marks, page?}), title_marks, authors, is_reference, similarity (hybrid/semantic), text_chars, has_note, highlight_count, projects. marks are [start, end) offsets in code points. relaxed: true means no paper contained every word and partial matches are shown. Ranking, weights and indexes: .specs/012_search.md.

docs.title: The Shared Layer Principle
docs.text:
The most important architectural rule in PaperManager:

db/queries/ and services/ are framework-neutral. Neither FastAPI nor MCP specifics leak into them. routers/ and tools/ are two different entry points over the same logic.

This means every capability is available both via HTTP (for the browser) and via MCP tool calls (for Claude Desktop), without any code duplication.

docs.title: Paper Ingestion Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant Router as routers/papers.py
    participant PDFParser as services/pdf_parser.py
    participant MetaLookup as services/metadata_lookup.py
    participant Drive as services/drive.py
    participant AI as services/ai.py
    participant DB as db/queries/papers.py
    participant Neo4j

    Browser->>Router: POST /papers/upload (PDF bytes)
    Router->>PDFParser: extract_text(pdf_bytes)
    PDFParser-->>Router: raw_text
    Router->>PDFParser: find_doi(raw_text)
    alt DOI found
        Router->>MetaLookup: lookup_semantic_scholar(doi)
        alt S2 fails
            Router->>MetaLookup: lookup_crossref(doi)
        end
    else No DOI
        Router->>PDFParser: extract_metadata_with_llm(raw_text[:3000])
        alt Ollama unavailable
            Router->>PDFParser: extract_metadata_heuristic(raw_text)
        end
    end
    Router->>Drive: upload_pdf(pdf_bytes)
    Drive-->>Router: drive_file_id
    Router->>AI: summarize_paper(abstract, raw_text)
    AI-->>Router: summary
    Router->>AI: extract_claims(raw_text)
    AI-->>Router: claims
    Router->>DB: create_paper(metadata + summary + drive_file_id)
    DB->>Neo4j: MERGE (p:Paper {...})
    Router->>DB: link_authors(paper_id, authors)
    Router->>DB: link_topics(paper_id, topics)
    Router-->>Browser: PaperOut JSON

docs.title: Key Design Decisions
docs.text:
See the full Decisions Log for rationale. The key principles:

  1. Neo4j over SQL — papers, people, topics, and tags are naturally a graph
  2. Tags as nodes — (Paper)-[:TAGGED]->(Tag) allows efficient "all papers with tag X" queries
  3. Topic ≠ Tag — Topics are formal research areas; Tags are free-form personal labels
  4. Notes as graph nodes — Notes have their own @mention and #topic relationships
  5. Shared service layer — MCP tools and HTTP routers call the same db/ and services/ code
  6. Prompts as files — All prompt templates live in prompts/ and are loaded fresh on each call
  7. Vector embeddings — Paper nodes store Ollama embeddings for semantic similarity search
  8. User identity — User nodes enable per-user conversation history and attribution

docs.title: main.py — App Entry Point
docs.text:
main.py creates the FastAPI application, sets up CORS, registers all routers, and defines a startup lifespan:

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    get_driver().verify_connectivity()   # verify Neo4j
    run_schema_setup(get_driver())       # create indexes + constraints
    seed_default_tags(get_driver())      # seed default tags
    seed_people_tags(get_driver())       # seed people-related tags
    yield

The app is started by start.sh via uvicorn backend.main:app.
