docs.title: Ingestion Workflow
docs.text: How papers enter the library, what runs when, and why.

docs.title: Stage 1 — Parse + preprocess + preanalyze (immediate, on drop)
docs.text:
Three requests start as soon as you drop a file. Nothing is saved.

1a — Metadata (POST /papers/parse)

Step What runs Cost Extract raw text pypdf local, fast Find DOI / arXiv ID regex on first page local, fast Metadata lookup Semantic Scholar → CrossRef API network LiteLLM fallback first 3 000 chars local, ~2 s Heuristics fallback first-line title, year regex local, instant Abstract extraction regex → Claude Haiku if needed conditional

1b — Layout (POST /papers/preprocess)

Step What runs Cost Docling figures + tables (once per PDF hash) GPU / slow

1c — Analysis (POST /papers/preanalyze) — the heavy LLM work, precomputed

Step What runs Cost summary summarize_paper (default instructions) LLM ai_topics suggest_topics LLM claims extract_claims LLM references extract_references LLM / network affiliations extract_affiliations_with_litellm LLM tag_suggestions suggest_tags_litellm LLM

Result: metadata pre-fills the modal; figures/tables and the full LLM analysis are cached on disk (keyed by PDF SHA-256). No paper is created.

The queue row turns green ("Ready — click to review") only once metadata, layout, and analysis are all ready — meaning Upload will be a pure save with no LLM work. The queue is persisted to IndexedDB and re-verified on return.

Normative spec: .specs/009_upload_queue_workflow.md

docs.title: Stage 2 — Confirm (modal, user-driven)
docs.text:
You open the modal, verify the pre-filled metadata, and pick the document type. Document type controls what runs in Stage 3:

Type Summary Figures References Paper (default) ✓ ✓ ✓ Book ✗ ✗ ✗ Lecture deck ✗ ✗ ✗

Nothing is saved until you click Upload →.

docs.title: Stage 3 — Upload (triggered on confirm)
docs.text:
Triggered by: POST /papers/upload Runs synchronously — the modal spinner shows while this completes.

PDF bytes
  │
  ├─ 0. load cached analysis      → analysis_key → result.json (no LLM)
  │
  ├─ 1. metadata                  → REUSE cached meta (else extract_metadata)
  │
  ├─ 2. title_override            → apply any title edit from the modal
  │
  ├─ 3. Drive upload              → stores PDF, returns drive_file_id
  │
  ├─ 4. summary                   → REUSE cached summary                     [PAPER only]
  │       re-runs summarize_paper ONLY if you edited the instructions
  │
  ├─ 5. embed_paper               → skipped unless litellm_embed_model is set
  │
  ├─ 6. save to Neo4j             → Paper node created (or stub enriched)
  │       duplicate check: 409 if paper with drive_file_id already exists
  │
  ├─ 7. link authors              → Person nodes, REUSE cached affiliations, S2 IDs
  │       7b. enrichment          → ORCID + S2 HTTP (not LLM, 24h cooldown)
  │
  ├─ 8. link topics              → Semantic Scholar topics + REUSE cached AI topics
  │
  ├─ 9. claims                   → REUSE cached claims                       [PAPER only]
  │
  ├─ 10. references              → REUSE cached references                   [PAPER only]
  │
  └─ 12. figures + tables        → reuse Stage 1b cache; upload images to Drive  [PAPER only]

With a fully-precomputed (green) row, Upload makes no LLM calls — everything is reused from the analysis cache. The only intentional LLM call is the summary, and only if you edited the summary instructions in the modal.

Where the Upload time goes: ~1–2 s Drive PDF upload + Neo4j writes + ORCID/S2 enrichment, then ~10–15 s uploading figure/table images to Google Drive (step 12). That last step is the bulk of the wait and is not precomputed by design.

Docling runs at most once per PDF: during Stage 1b (queue) when possible; upload step 12 only runs Docling if preprocess failed or was skipped.

docs.title: Stage 4 — Onboarding (modal, user-driven)
docs.text:
After the upload completes the modal walks through:

  1. References — review extracted references, uncheck any to skip
  2. Tags — AI-suggested + your existing tags, add custom ones
  3. Project — optionally assign to a project
  4. People — link supervisor / colleague / who shared it

These steps are purely interactive and make no AI calls.

docs.title: Why extract_metadata runs twice
docs.text:
Stage 1 (/papers/parse) extracts metadata to pre-fill the modal. Stage 3 (/papers/upload) needs to re-run it because the raw text is required for the summary and is too large to pass through the frontend. The Stage 1 result is discarded client-side after filling the form.

Consequence: Ollama + S2 API calls happen twice per paper. Summary and figures happen once.

docs.title: URL Ingest
docs.text:
Triggered by: POST /papers/from-url-full

URL
  │
  ├─ resolve metadata (arXiv API / S2 / CrossRef / PubMed)
  │
  ├─ download PDF (arXiv / bioRxiv only — others blocked by Cloudflare)
  │
  ├─ [if PDF available]
  │     ├─ extract_metadata from PDF
  │     ├─ Drive upload
  │     ├─ summarize_paper (full text)
  │     ├─ save to Neo4j
  │     ├─ extract references
  │     └─ extract figures
  │
  └─ [if no PDF]
        ├─ summarize_paper (abstract only — shorter, weaker)
        └─ save to Neo4j (no drive_file_id, no raw_text)

Modal still shows refs → tags → project → people onboarding after this completes.

docs.title: Duplicate handling
docs.text:
Scenario Outcome Same DOI / title in queue, not yet uploaded Both show "Ready". First to upload wins; second gets 409 in the modal. Paper already in library (has PDF) Caught in Stage 1 duplicate check → queue row shows "Already in your library" Paper exists as a stub (URL-ingested, no PDF) Upload enriches the stub with full text, new summary, figures. Old abstract-based summary is replaced.

The stub enrichment case is the only scenario where a summary is regenerated — and it's intentional: the full-text summary from Stage 3 is better than the abstract-only summary from URL ingest.

docs.title: Book / Lecture Deck
docs.text:
When you select Book or Lecture Deck in the modal:

  • Steps 4, 9, 10, 11 (summary, claims, references, figures) are all skipped
  • Tags book or lecture_deck are applied automatically
  • Chapter structure can be detected afterwards via Chapters tab on the paper detail page

docs.title: Manual operations (on-demand, never automatic)
docs.text:
These only run when you explicitly trigger them from the paper detail page:

Action Endpoint What it does Regenerate summary POST /{id}/regenerate-summary Re-runs Claude summary on stored raw_text Re-extract abstract POST /{id}/reextract-abstract Regex + Claude Haiku on raw_text Re-extract references GET /{id}/ai-extract-references Forces Claude Haiku reference extraction Extract figures triggered from Figures tab Re-runs Docling / pypdf pipeline

docs.title: Conference explorer
docs.text: The Conferences tab browses the accepted papers of the major ML, vision, NLP and robotics conferences two ways: by institution (where does a university, lab or company rank, what does it publish on, with whom) and by topic (type a topic or paste an abstract: which universities and companies publish most on it, and which papers are closest). It works for every conference-year in the list below, not one fixed conference, and runs entirely on your own server. A search box on the landing page searches all loaded conferences at once: papers, authors and where a topic is published.

docs.title: Which conferences
docs.text:
Field Conferences Source ML NeurIPS 2020–2026, ICML 2022–2026, ICLR 2022–2026 official conference site ML AISTATS, UAI, COLT Paper Copilot Vision CVPR 2023–2026, ICCV 2025, ECCV 2024 and 2026 official conference site Vision CVPR 2022, ICCV 2021/2023, ECCV 2022, WACV Paper Copilot NLP ACL, EMNLP, NAACL, COLM Paper Copilot General AI AAAI, IJCAI Paper Copilot Robotics CoRL, RSS, ICRA, IROS Paper Copilot Data KDD, WWW Paper Copilot

Official conference sites. NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, CVPR, ICCV and ECCV publish every accepted paper as one JSON file, with authors, each author's institution (92–98 % of authors carry one), abstract, decision (poster, spotlight, oral), session and the OpenReview link.

Paper Copilot keeps paper lists for the other venues and older years. Most come with normalised affiliations; a few (ACL 2025, recent OpenReview venues that hide them) do not, and for those the page says the institution views are thin and the topic view is the useful one. Rejected and withdrawn submissions are dropped.

Some sites serve only the first page of their list without a login (CVPR 2026 at the time of writing: 199 of 5,163 papers with authors). The titles of the rest come from the site's public paper list, so topic search still covers the whole conference, and the page says for how many papers institutions are known.

docs.title: Loading a conference
docs.text:
The first time you open a conference that is not loaded, PaperManager downloads its list and indexes it in the background; the page shows the progress and fills in as it goes:

  1. Downloading the list (a few seconds).
  2. Reading: institution names are normalised and counted. The institution views work from here on.
  3. Indexing: every title and abstract is embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5 on the CPU, which gives the research areas and semantic topic search. About two minutes for NeurIPS 2026 (6,500 papers, titles only so far); with abstracts 7–15 minutes (ACL 2025, 3,100 papers: 7 min; NeurIPS 2025, 5,900 papers: 14 min) on four CPU threads. A conference with abstracts or keywords also gets its titles embedded on their own (20–45 s), which the cross-conference search compares conferences on.

A default set is loaded when the backend starts (see Settings), so the main conferences are ready without anyone waiting. refresh at the bottom of a conference page downloads it again; this year's conferences are also refreshed automatically every two weeks, since the sites keep adding abstracts, sessions and late papers until the meeting.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Paper count, institution count and the share of papers with at least one company author; the research-area mix of the whole conference (click an area for its institution ranking); the top universities and institutes, and the top companies.

docs.title: Institutions
docs.text:
A ranked table of every institution, searchable by name, filterable by academia / industry and by research area. With an area selected the table ranks by papers in that area and shows what share of each institution's own papers that area is ("of own").

Click a row for the institution card:

  • Rank overall and among universities or companies, papers, fractional papers and share of the conference.
  • Research areas against the whole conference: the thin bar under the institution's bar is the conference's mix, and areas the institution publishes in at least twice the conference rate are marked ×2.0, ×3.1, ...
  • Most frequent co-authoring institutions and the authors with the most papers there.
  • Every paper, orals and spotlights first; click an area in the legend to filter.

docs.title: Topics & papers
docs.text:
Type a topic ("RL for LLM reasoning", "diffusion models for protein structure") or paste a whole abstract. The query is embedded with the same model, the closest 50 / 100 / 200 / 500 papers are taken, and the page shows:

  • their research-area mix and how many have a company author;
  • the universities & institutes and the companies with the most of those papers (hover for what share of the institution's papers at the conference that is);
  • the closest papers, each with its match score, area, decision, session and institutions.

Short queries get bge's retrieval instruction ("Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ..."); a pasted abstract is embedded as is. Until a conference is indexed, topic search falls back to keyword matching on titles and abstracts and says so.

Short queries go into the URL (/conferences/neurips2026?view=topics&q=video%20generation), so a result can be shared or bookmarked.

docs.title: Papers and your library
docs.text: Every paper row shows In library when a paper with the same title is already in your library (it links to it), and + Library otherwise. Adding creates the paper with its title, abstract, venue ("NeurIPS 2026"), year and authors (each with their institution as affiliation), tagged from-conference. Upload the PDF later from the paper page for the full pipeline. Click a title for the abstract, the author list with institutions and the eight closest papers at the same conference; ↗ opens the paper on the conference site.

docs.title: Searching all conferences
docs.text:
The search box at the top of the Conferences page searches every loaded conference at once. Type a title, an author or a topic, or paste an abstract; results update 300 ms after you stop typing. Three tabs show three readings of the same query; the page opens the one that fits (an author's name that matches no title opens Authors, a text of more than twelve words opens Topics, anything else Papers). Filters narrow the search to a field (ML, Vision, NLP, ...), a series (NeurIPS) or a range of years. Query, tab and filters are kept in the URL (/conferences?q=Charlotte%20Deane&kind=author), so a search can be shared or bookmarked. A tab you pick stays picked for the next query.

Capital and small letters never matter, nor do accents: CHARLOTTE DEANE, charlotte deane and Charlotte Déane give the same results. Matched words are marked in titles and names. When a word looks like a typo, the page asks "Did you mean ...?" (the results already include the corrected word).

Keys: Enter searches at once, Esc clears the box (or returns to it from a result), ↑ / ↓ move through the results, Enter on a result opens it.

docs.title: Papers
docs.text:
• Title matches: titles containing the query's words, best first: the whole title, then titles starting with the query, then the query as a phrase, then all its words in any order, then (for queries of three words or more) all but one. A word also matches its plural, the last word matches as a prefix while you type it ("video gen"), and a word of five letters or more matches with one typo ("difusion"). Ties are broken by closeness in meaning.
  • Closest by meaning: the papers whose titles are nearest to the query in embedding space and that did not already match by words. A typo is corrected before embedding.

Each paper carries a chip with its conference; it expands, links and goes into your library as anywhere else in the explorer.

docs.title: Authors
docs.text:
Names are matched with case and accents folded, by full name, surname, "Surname, First", initials (c deane), the start of a name or with one typo. Each author card shows the number of papers, conferences and distinct co-authors, the institutions given on those papers, and the papers grouped by conference, newest first, each with the author's position and their institution on that paper.

A name is not a person: two researchers can share one. When an author's papers fall into groups that share neither an institution nor a co-author, the card says so and lists the groups ("may belong to 2 people: Tsinghua University · Stanford University").

docs.title: Topics
docs.text:
Type a topic or paste an abstract to see where it is published:

  • Per conference: how many of the closest papers each conference holds, per 1,000 of its papers, so a conference of 2,700 papers compares with one of 6,600.
  • Over the years: the same rate for every series loaded for more than one year (NeurIPS 2025 → 2026), with the change.
  • Universities & institutes and companies counted over all conferences together (hover for the count per conference), and the research-area mix of those papers.
  • Closest papers over all conferences.

"Closest" means the 100 / 300 / 1,000 papers nearest to the query among all papers of all selected conferences together. The similarity of the last of them is one threshold for every conference, shown under the heading.

Conferences are compared on title embeddings only. A title-plus-abstract embedding sits 0.03–0.07 higher in cosine similarity to any query than a title-only one, so NeurIPS 2025 (with abstracts) would otherwise hold five times as many "diffusion models for protein structure" papers per 1,000 as NeurIPS 2026 (titles only so far) when the papers' titles say they are about equally common. For this reason the numbers differ from a single conference's Topics & papers view, which uses titles and abstracts.

Example, all nine default conferences, closest 300: "diffusion models for protein structure" is densest at ICLR 2026 (12.1 per 1,000) and NeurIPS 2025 (12.0), then ICML 2026 (8.7) and NeurIPS 2026 (7.4); MIT and Google lead with 19 papers each. "video generation" is densest at ECCV 2026, CVPR 2026 and ICCV 2025 (14–17 per 1,000, against 4–7 at the ML venues), with ByteDance (33) and Alibaba (26) the top companies.

Search all conferences → next to a single conference's topic result runs the same query here.

docs.title: How things are counted
docs.text:
• Papers: a paper counts once for every institution with at least one author on it. A paper by MIT and Google counts for both.
  • Fractional: each author is 1/n of a paper (n authors), split equally over that author's institutions. Fractional counts sum to the number of papers with affiliations.
  • Rank: by papers, ties share a rank.
  • Institution names are normalised: HTML entities and full-width letters are cleaned, department names dropped ("Department of Computer Science, ETH Zurich" → ETH Zurich), several affiliations in one field split ("Google, TUM" → Google and TU Munich), and spellings merged. About 220 alias rules merge the common cases: Google with DeepMind, Meta with FAIR, the institutes of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, campus spellings ("University of California, Berkeley", "UC Berkeley"), acronyms (MIT, CMU, KAIST, EPFL). Everything else keeps its own spelling and is merged by case, accents and punctuation.
  • Academia / industry: aliases carry it; otherwise a name with "university", "institute", "college", "laboratory", "hospital", ... is academia, anything else a company. Non-profit institutes (Allen Institute for AI, Mila, Max Planck, Shanghai AI Laboratory) count as academia. "Independent researcher" is not counted, nor are placeholders and fragments the sources contain: anonymised names ("AXXX", "Anonymous Institution"), bare words ("University", "ML", "Research"), names of one or two letters without an alias ("HY"; "LG" and "HP" are aliases), e-mail addresses and web addresses of universities. "Head of AI @ Squirrel AI" counts as Squirrel AI.
  • Research areas are one fixed taxonomy of 24 areas for every conference, so the mix of NeurIPS and ICML can be compared and an area keeps its colour everywhere. Each paper gets the area whose description is closest to its embedding, after both are centred on the conference's mean paper vector; the area centres are then moved halfway towards their papers twice. Areas are a coarse map, not a label: a paper on, say, RL for theorem proving lands in one area only.

A wrong institution mapping is fixed by an alias line in backend/services/conferences/institutions.py.

docs.title: From Claude (MCP)
docs.text:
Five MCP tools expose the same data to Claude Desktop and Claude Code:

Tool Answers list_conferences Which conference-years are loaded, with paper and institution counts conference_topic Who publishes on a topic at a conference: top universities and companies, area mix, closest papers. With conference="all": the same over every loaded conference, plus papers per 1,000 per conference and the trend over years conference_institution What one institution published at a conference: rank, counts, area mix against the conference, collaborators, authors, papers conference_search_papers Papers across all loaded conferences by title words (typos tolerated), then by meaning conference_search_author An author across all loaded conferences: papers per conference with their institution on each, co-author count, and whether the name looks like more than one person

conference takes a key (neurips2026), a name (ICML 2025), a bare series (iclr = its latest year) or, for conference_topic, all. Papers already in your library come back with their library_paper_id.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
All optional; set them in .env and pass them to the backend in docker-compose.yml.

Variable Default What it does CONFERENCES_AUTO true Load the default conferences at startup CONFERENCES_DEFAULT neurips2026,icml2026,iclr2026,cvpr2026,iccv2025,eccv2026,neurips2025,acl2025 Which ones CONFERENCES_REFRESH_DAYS 14 Reload this year's default conferences when older than this CONFERENCE_DATA_DIR /data/conferences Where datasets and the model live (the backend's volume) CONFERENCE_EMBED_THREADS 4 CPU threads for embedding CONFERENCE_CACHE_MAX 32 Conferences held in memory at once (20–40 MB each); searching all conferences needs every loaded one in memory

Each conference takes 5–30 MB on disk (papers, institutions, float16 embeddings); the model takes 130 MB once. No API key is involved and nothing is sent anywhere except the download of the paper lists and, once, the model.

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
This page takes one paper from upload to concept map. It assumes PaperManager is already running and you can log in; if not, start with Hosting your own.

Plan about ten minutes, most of it waiting for the AI steps to finish in the background.

docs.title: 1. Add a paper
docs.text:
1. Open Library (the first item in the top menu).
  2. Click + (Add paper). Drag a PDF into the drop zone, or paste a link such as https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364.
  3. PaperManager looks up title, authors, year and DOI on Semantic Scholar and CrossRef. A badge shows where the details came from; yellow or red means please check.
  4. Fix anything that is wrong and confirm.

The paper appears in your library straight away. Summary, topics, figures and references are added in the background over the next minute or two.

Many papers at once

Drop several PDFs at once, or click + → Import multiple papers at once and paste a list of DOIs, arXiv IDs or URLs. See Ingesting papers.

docs.title: 2. Open it and read
docs.text:
Click the paper. The view has two halves:

Left side Right side PDF, abstract, summary, figures, tables, references, related papers, claims Notes, Chat, Highlights, Concepts, Tour

Try these in order:

  • Summary (left): the AI summary of the whole paper.
  • Figures (left): every figure with its caption; ask a question about one.
  • Chat (right): ask anything about this paper, e.g. "What is the main limitation?"
  • Highlights: select text in the PDF to highlight it in a colour; highlights are listed here.

docs.title: 3. Let it explain the paper
docs.text:
Two tabs on the right help with hard papers. Both are explained in Concepts, tour and concept map.

  • Tour → Make a quick tour. You get an overview, a list of sections you can skip, and 6–12 stops. Click a stop (or use ← / →) and the PDF jumps to the passage it is about.
  • Concepts → Find concepts. PaperManager marks ideas on the PDF pages that a picture explains better than text, and draws an animation, plot or formula breakdown for each one.

docs.title: 4. Put it in a project
docs.text:
1. Open Projects, type a name and click Create.
  2. In the project, use Search library to add a paper… to add your paper (and a few more).
  3. Click Concept map. Each paper's key concepts are extracted and joined into one graph. Concepts shared by several papers grow larger; the filters narrow it by author, year or kind of concept.

docs.title: 5. Ask across everything
docs.text:
Open Knowledge in the top menu and ask a question, for example:

@project:MyThesis Which papers compare against diffusion baselines, and how do they differ?

The answer cites the papers it used. Leave out the @project: part to search the whole library, or turn on web search for questions your papers do not cover. More in Knowledge features.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Library: search, filters and views
  • Reading a paper: every tab of the paper view
  • MCP server: use your library from Claude Desktop or Claude Code

docs.title: Local development
docs.text: This page sets PaperManager up from source, with the backend and frontend running directly on your machine so code changes show up immediately. To simply use PaperManager, the Docker setup in Hosting your own is quicker.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Requirement Version Notes Python 3.11+ Use conda or pyenv Node.js 18+ For the frontend Neo4j 5.x Local Docker container (below) or a free AuraDB instance Google account — Google Drive for PDF storage Anthropic API key — Claude for summaries & chat Ollama (optional) latest Local AI for metadata extraction

docs.title: 1 — Clone the repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/NiklasAbraham/PaperManager
cd PaperManager

docs.title: 2 — Set up the Python environment
docs.text:
conda create -n papermanager python=3.11 -y
conda activate papermanager
pip install -r backend/requirements.txt

docs.title: 3 — Install the frontend
docs.text:
cd frontend
npm install
cd ..

docs.title: 4 — Install Ollama (optional, recommended)
docs.text:
Ollama is used for local metadata extraction (layer 2), tag suggestions, Cypher assist, and figure captions. Without it the system still works using Semantic Scholar and Claude.

# macOS
brew install ollama

# Linux
curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh

# Pull the model
ollama pull llama3.2:3b

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Copy the example environment file and fill in your credentials:

cp .env.example .env

Edit .env:

# ── Neo4j ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
NEO4J_URI=bolt://localhost:7687
NEO4J_USER=neo4j
NEO4J_PASSWORD=your-password

# ── Google Drive ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# OAuth desktop app credentials from Google Cloud Console
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=xxxx.apps.googleusercontent.com
GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=xxxx
GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID=xxxx   # Folder where PDFs will be stored

# ── Anthropic ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-xxxx

# Anthropic Foundry enterprise gateway (optional)
ANTHROPIC_WORK_API_KEY=xxxx
ANTHROPIC_WORK_BASE_URL=https://your-foundry-gateway.com/...

# ── App ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
BACKEND_PORT=8000
FRONTEND_URL=http://localhost:5173

# ── Ollama ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OLLAMA_MODEL=llama3.2:3b

# ── Corporate network (optional) ──────────────────────────────
SSL_VERIFY=true
SSL_CA_BUNDLE=/path/to/corporate-ca.pem

docs.title: Neo4j setup
docs.text:
The quickest option is a local container:

docker run -d --name papermanager-neo4j -p 7687:7687 -p 7474:7474 \
  -e NEO4J_AUTH=neo4j/change-me neo4j:5

Then set NEO4J_URI=bolt://localhost:7687, NEO4J_USER=neo4j and NEO4J_PASSWORD=change-me in .env. A free AuraDB instance works too: copy its neo4j+s:// URI and credentials instead.

docs.title: Google Drive setup
docs.text:
1. Go to Google Cloud Console
  2. Create a project and enable the Google Drive API
  3. Create OAuth 2.0 credentials (Desktop application type)
  4. Download the credentials JSON
  5. On first backend start, a browser window opens for OAuth authorisation
  6. Credentials are saved to backend/token.json and reused automatically

docs.title: Starting the Application
docs.text:
./start.sh

This script:

  • Starts the FastAPI backend on port 8000 (logs → /tmp/papermanager-backend.log)
  • Starts the Vite frontend on port 5173 (logs → /tmp/papermanager-frontend.log)
  • Optionally starts Ollama if configured

Open http://localhost:5173 in your browser.

Checking logs

tail -f /tmp/papermanager-backend.log
tail -f /tmp/papermanager-frontend.log

docs.title: First Run
docs.text:
On startup the backend automatically:

  1. Verifies the Neo4j connection
  2. Runs schema setup (creates indexes and constraints)
  3. Seeds 157 default tags across source, workflow, content, and domain categories

You should see the library page with a drop zone and a + button to add papers.

docs.title: Demo data
docs.text:
To try the app before adding your own papers, load the demo library into your local development database:

cd backend
python scripts/seed_demo.py                  # your login (DEFAULT_USER_NAME) joins the demo projects
python scripts/seed_demo.py --member alice   # or name the login(s) that should see them

It adds ten well-known papers (Attention Is All You Need, DDPM, Score SDE, EDM, Flow Matching, AlphaFold 2 and 3, RFdiffusion, ESM-2 and a GNN survey) with their authors, topics, tags and citations, two projects, notes with @mentions and #topics, claims, a project concept map and a conversation. It is the same data the tests use (backend/tests/fixtures/demo_library.json). The script only adds data, does nothing when the demo is already loaded, and refuses a Neo4j that is not on this machine unless you pass --force.

docs.title: Running the tests
docs.text:
backend/scripts/run_tests.sh                          # everything except @integration tests
backend/scripts/run_tests.sh -q tests/test_search.py  # any pytest arguments

The script starts a throwaway Neo4j and runs pytest in a one-off container of the backend image (build it first with docker compose build backend), on a Docker network with no route to the internet, then removes both. Your .env is not used. Tests that would reach an outside service fail and name the host; tests that really need one (Anthropic, Google Drive) are marked @pytest.mark.integration and are left out by default.

Tests write to the database, so they refuse to run against a Neo4j that is not on this machine unless PM_TESTS_ALLOW_DB=1 says it is disposable. Never point them at your real library. Tests that need a populated graph use the demo_library fixture, which empties the test database and loads the demo library.

docs.title: What's Next?
docs.text:
• First steps — one paper from upload to concept map
  • Ingest your first paper — drag a PDF or paste a URL
  • Browse the library — search, filter, sort your papers
  • Chat with a paper — ask Claude questions about any paper
  • Explore the knowledge graph — visualise connections

docs.title: Ingesting Papers
docs.text: PaperManager supports three ways to add papers to your library.

docs.title: PDF Upload
docs.text: Drag a PDF onto the Library page or click the + button → PDF tab.

docs.title: What Happens Automatically
docs.text:
The upload follows a multi-step pipeline:

flowchart TD
    A[📄 PDF uploaded] --> B[Extract text with Docling]
    B --> C{DOI / arXiv ID\nin text?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Semantic Scholar API]
    D -->|Not found| E[CrossRef API]
    C -->|No title found| F[Ollama LLM on first 3 000 chars]
    F -->|Ollama unavailable| G[Regex heuristics]
    D --> H[Confirmation modal]
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H -->|User confirms| I[Upload PDF to Google Drive]
    I --> J[Create Paper node in Neo4j]
    J --> K[Generate AI summary — Claude Opus]
    K --> L[Suggest topics — Claude Haiku]
    L --> M[Extract references]
    M --> N[Extract figures from PDF]
    N --> O[✅ Paper ready in library]

docs.title: Step-by-Step: The Upload Modal
docs.text:
After choosing a PDF you walk through up to five optional steps (each can be toggled in Settings):

  1. Metadata confirmation — review extracted title, year, authors, DOI, venue; fix any errors
  2. Source — record how you found this paper (person, LinkedIn, Twitter, conference, newsletter…)
  3. Summary prompt — edit the Claude prompt before the AI summary is generated
  4. References review — approve which references to save as CITES links
  5. Tags — review AI-suggested tags before saving

docs.title: Upload Modal Options
docs.text: Option Default Description Source step on Record how you found the paper Summary prompt step on Edit the AI summary instructions Auto-save references off Skip review and save all references automatically Tags step on Review AI-suggested tags before saving

docs.title: Metadata Source Badge
docs.text:
After upload each paper card shows a colour-coded badge:

Colour Source 🟢 Green Semantic Scholar or CrossRef 🟡 Yellow Ollama LLM extraction 🔴 Red Heuristic guess

docs.title: URL / DOI Ingest
docs.text:
Click + → URL / DOI tab. Paste any of:

Input format Example arXiv URL https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762 arXiv ID 1706.03762 or arXiv:1706.03762 DOI URL https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14539 Bare DOI 10.1038/nature14539 PubMed URL https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12345678/ bioRxiv URL https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/... medRxiv URL https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/...

docs.title: What Happens
docs.text:
1. The URL/ID is parsed to detect the source type
  2. Metadata is fetched from the appropriate API (arXiv Atom, Semantic Scholar, CrossRef, PubMed eUtils, bioRxiv)
  3. If a DOI is found, Semantic Scholar is queried for richer data (citation count, affiliations, topics)
  4. Paper is auto-tagged from-url
  5. No PDF is stored — the paper is metadata-only

Note

To get a PDF for a URL-ingested paper, open the Paper Detail page and click Upload PDF.

docs.title: Bulk Import
docs.text:
Go to Bulk Import in the nav bar. Upload or paste a JSON file:

{
  "fetch_pdf": true,
  "project_id": "optional-project-uuid",
  "papers": [
    {"url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762"},
    {"arxiv": "1810.04805"},
    {"doi": "10.1038/nature14539"},
    {"url": "https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30082513/"},
    {"title": "AlphaFold protein structure prediction"},
    {"title": "CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing", "fetch_pdf": false}
  ]
}

Each entry needs at least one of: url, arxiv, doi, title. Formats can be mixed freely.

A sample file is included at sample_bulk_import.json.

docs.title: Resolution Order
docs.text:
For each paper entry the system tries, in order:

flowchart LR
    E1["url → URL resolver"] --> E2["arxiv → arXiv API"]
    E2 --> E3["doi → S2 → CrossRef"]
    E3 --> E4["title → S2 title search\n→ arXiv title search\n→ Ollama-improved arXiv"]

docs.title: PDF Fetching
docs.text:
When fetch_pdf: true:

  • arXiv papers — downloaded from arxiv.org/pdf/{id}
  • Other papers — Unpaywall API checked for an open-access PDF URL

docs.title: Progress Stream
docs.text:
Bulk import shows a live log stream as papers are processed. Papers that already exist by DOI are reported as "skipped". All imported papers are auto-tagged bulk-import.

Project assignment

Set "project_id" in the JSON to automatically add all imported papers to a project.

docs.title: Duplicate Detection
docs.text:
Before a paper is saved, a duplicate check runs against existing papers:

  • Exact DOI match → blocked (the paper already exists)
  • High title similarity → warning shown in the confirmation modal

If a DOI-matched stub already exists (from reference extraction), the stub is enriched with full metadata rather than creating a duplicate.

docs.title: Knowledge Features
docs.text: PaperManager includes three advanced knowledge tools: an interactive graph, a multi-paper AI chat, and a direct Cypher query editor.

docs.title: Knowledge Graph
docs.text: Navigate to Graph in the nav bar for an interactive WebGL visualisation of your entire library.

docs.title: Node Types
docs.text: Colour Node type 🟣 Purple Paper 🔵 Blue Person 🟢 Green Topic 🟠 Orange Tag 🩷 Pink Project ⚫ Grey Note

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
• Pan — click and drag the background
  • Zoom — scroll or pinch
  • Move nodes — drag individual nodes
  • Click a node — opens a properties panel on the right:
  • View all node properties
  • Navigate to the paper detail page
  • Delete the node

docs.title: Graph Modes
docs.text:
Mode What is shown Full graph All node types (up to 500 nodes) Papers only Papers, People, Topics Single paper One paper with all its direct neighbours

Switch modes using the toggle in the top-left of the graph.

docs.title: Display Options
docs.text:
Use the sliders and toggles in the control panel to adjust:

  • Node size
  • Link distance
  • Repulsion force
  • Show / hide node labels
  • Show / hide edge labels

docs.title: Knowledge Chat
docs.text: Navigate to Knowledge in the nav bar to ask questions across your whole library. The page has three parts: your conversations on the left, the chat in the middle, and a preview pane on the right that opens when you click a cited paper or a figure.

docs.title: Asking
docs.text:
Type a question and press Enter (Shift+Enter for a new line). Without a scope, the chat finds relevant papers by semantic search and adds the most recent ones. To choose the context yourself:

In the composer What is loaded @project:my-phd-papers Papers in that project @topic:Protein Folding Papers about that topic @tag:deep-learning Papers with that tag @paper:Attention is All You Need Papers whose title matches @person:lecun Papers by or involving that person @user:alice Asks a teammate's conversations instead of the library + paper Attaches one library paper; it is always in context

Typing @ suggests projects, topics, tags, people and papers; the scopes you use show as chips above the text. While the model works, the steps it takes (graph queries, searches, reading a paper's full text, listing its figures, searching the web) appear as rows above the answer; click one to see the query or the papers it found. Stop ends an answer early.

The bar under the text holds web (allow web search), concepts (make concept cards for every answer), and the model: Claude with your API key, Claude Code on a Claude subscription (if the server owner enabled it for you), Claude (Work), or the self-hosted LiteLLM model.

docs.title: Answers
docs.text:
Answers render maths, code, tables and figures from your papers. Library papers are cited as violet links: click one to open its summary, abstract, figures and PDF beside the chat, or Open in library for the full paper page. Under each answer you see the papers it cited and how many were in context.

Concept cards. Press ✦ Visualise under an answer (or switch concepts to auto) and the app finds the ideas in the answer that a picture would explain, then attaches an interactive card at the end of the section that discusses each: a formula walked through step by step, a graph, a short sourced note, or an animation with pause, play, speed (0.5×, 1×, 2×) and replay. Formulas and graphs take about a minute, animations a few. If an animation breaks, fix asks the model to repair it. The cards are saved with the conversation.

3D structures. When a question is about a protein or another molecule, the answer can show it in 3D: an experimental structure from the PDB, or an AlphaFold DB prediction coloured by confidence (pLDDT). Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, hover to name a residue, click residues to collect them; the card has surface, spin, reset, fullscreen and PNG export, and chips that toggle the highlighted regions. Asking for a structure by its PDB id ("show 6VXX and highlight the receptor-binding domain") works well.

docs.title: Conversations and strands
docs.text:
Conversations are saved automatically and listed newest first; search them, rename or delete them on hover, and start a new one with + New. compact summarises older turns to free up context in a long conversation.

Hover one of your questions to fork the conversation: ⑂ edit starts a copy just before that question with its text back in the composer, ⑂ strand continues a copy from that answer. The original stays as it was. Strands are nested under their conversation in the list, and the line beside the transcript shows where each one left; click its knob to open it, or the ↑ link above the title to go back.

docs.title: Example prompts
docs.text:
@topic:Protein Folding How has the approach changed from RoseTTAFold to AlphaFold 3?

Explain the denoising score-matching objective behind diffusion models, with the derivation.

Show the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (6VXX) in 3D and highlight the receptor-binding domain.

@project:my-phd-papers Summarise the key open problems.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The strip above the chat shows how much of the model's context window the question uses, split into system prompt, papers, conversation, question and answer. Click it to see which papers are in context.

flowchart TD
    Q["Question"] --> P["Scopes and attached papers"]
    P -->|"Scoped"| C["Graph queries fetch the papers"]
    P -->|"No scope"| R["Semantic search + recent papers"]
    C --> A["Papers with your notes and earlier chats"]
    R --> A
    A --> M["Model answers, using library tools as needed"]
    M --> V["Optional: concept cards from the answer"]

docs.title: Cypher Editor
docs.text: Navigate to Cypher in the nav bar for direct access to the Neo4j database.

docs.title: Schema Browser
docs.text:
A live view of all:

  • Node labels and their property keys
  • Relationship types
  • Fulltext indexes

docs.title: Query Editor
docs.text: Write and run raw Cypher queries. Results are shown in a table. Mutation counters show nodes created/deleted, relationships created/deleted, and properties set. Maximum 500 rows are returned.

docs.title: AI Assist
docs.text: Describe what you want in plain English — Ollama generates the Cypher query for you. You can then review and run it.

docs.title: Example Queries
docs.text:
-- Papers citing a specific paper
MATCH (a:Paper)-[:CITES]->(b:Paper {title: "..."})
RETURN a.title, a.year

-- Most connected authors
MATCH (p:Person)<-[:AUTHORED_BY]-(paper:Paper)
RETURN p.name, count(paper) AS papers ORDER BY papers DESC LIMIT 10

-- Papers without summaries
MATCH (p:Paper) WHERE p.summary IS NULL RETURN p.title, p.year

-- All papers on a topic
MATCH (p:Paper)-[:ABOUT]->(t:Topic {name: "Transformers"})
RETURN p.title, p.year ORDER BY p.year DESC

-- Papers shared by a colleague
MATCH (person:Person {name: "Jan"})<-[:INVOLVES {role: "shared_by"}]-(p:Paper)
RETURN p.title, p.year

docs.title: People
docs.text:
Navigate to People in the nav bar.

Contributed by Antoine Luciano

Surname order, the CV tab and the duplicate finder come from Antoine Luciano (#36).

All people in the system are listed in the sidebar with search, sorted by surname ("Christian P. Robert" under R; a particle stays with the given names, so "Aad van der Vaart" is under V).

Person detail shows:

  • Name and affiliation
  • Papers where they are an author (AUTHORED_BY)
  • Papers where they have an INVOLVES role (shared_by, working_on, collaborating, etc.)

  • Research specialties (linked Topic nodes via SPECIALIZES)

  • CV tab: current position, education, past affiliations, h-index, citations, topics and most cited works, built by ↻ CV from OpenAlex, ORCID, Wikidata (photo, homepage) and the person's homepage. Before trusting a profile it checks the person is really an author of their papers in the library; a profile found by name alone is accepted only if it lists one of those papers, since common names have many homonyms. The status dot says how it went: green (consistent with the library papers), amber (mostly), red (probably a homonym or a wrong author link), grey (no profile found).

Settings → People chooses the model that reads homepages (CV model: the server's fast model, e.g. Gemma via LiteLLM, or Claude Haiku / Opus on your Anthropic key) and has Build missing CVs, which builds a CV for every author without one, in the background and a few seconds apart. The profile data itself comes from OpenAlex, ORCID and Wikidata and needs no key.

People are auto-created when papers are ingested from the author list.

docs.title: Duplicate people
docs.text: The same researcher often arrives under several spellings ("Alán Aspuru-Guzik" and "Al'an Aspuru-Guzik", "Nele P. Quast" and "Nele Quast", "C. P. Robert" and "Christian P. Robert"). ⧉ Dups at the top of the sidebar lists the groups that look like one person, with the rule that linked them. Pick which one to keep (the one with a Semantic Scholar id or the most papers is preselected) and Merge, or Merge all. The kept person gets every paper, tag and note of the others, fills its empty fields from theirs, and keeps their names as aliases. An initial is joined to a full name only when one full name fits ("C. Robert" stays alone next to both "Christian Robert" and "Claire Robert"). backend/scripts/merge_people.py applies the same rules from the command line.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Navigate to Projects in the nav bar.

Create named collections of papers:

  • Create a project with name, description, and status (active / paused / done)
  • Add/remove papers from a project
  • Papers can belong to multiple projects
  • Filter the library by project
  • Link projects as related (RELATED_TO)
  • Select a project during upload, URL ingest, or bulk import to add papers automatically

docs.title: Export
docs.text: Format How BibTeX GET /export/bibtex — downloads a .bib file containing all papers JSON Available from the Settings page

docs.title: Backfill (Bulk Enrichment)
docs.text:
Run from the Settings page or directly via the API:

Operation Endpoint Description Backfill topics POST /backfill/topics Run Claude Haiku topic suggestion on all papers without topics Backfill summaries POST /backfill/summary Generate AI summaries for papers that have raw_text but no summary Backfill figures POST /backfill/figures Extract figures from all papers that have a PDF but no figures yet

Each returns {processed, skipped, errors}.

docs.title: Library
docs.text: The Library is the main page of PaperManager (/). It shows all papers in your collection and provides powerful search and filtering tools.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
When no filters are active you see a dashboard at the top showing:

  • Count cards — total papers, authors, topics, tags, projects
  • Papers by year bar chart
  • Top topics list
  • Recently added papers

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Type in the search box at the top. Results appear as you type (250 ms after the last keystroke, or at once on Enter), ranked by relevance, and every row says why it matched: chips such as Title, Author: Tero Karras, Topic: Diffusion Models, Your note, Highlight, Full text or Meaning 0.78, and one or two passages with the matched words marked.

docs.title: What is searched
docs.text:
Where Weight DOI or arXiv id typed as the query exact match, always first Title highest; extra when every word or the whole query is in the title Authors high; a query that is someone's name puts their papers first Your notes and your PDF highlights (with their comments) high Topics, tags medium Abstract, AI summary, extracted claims medium Venue low Extracted full text of the PDF lowest (every word must occur in it)

A paper has to contain every word of the query somewhere in those fields (one word in the author list and another in the title is fine). If no paper does, the papers that contain some of the words are shown with a note saying so. Papers cited by many other papers in your library rank a little higher among equally good matches.

Case and accents never matter: edm, EDM and Edm find the same papers, as do Kynkaanniemi and Kynkäänniemi, in the search, the suggestions and the filters.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
You type It finds diffusion diffusion, diffusions, Diffusion-based (every word is also a prefix) diffus* any word starting with diffus scroe based score-based: words of 5+ letters tolerate one typo "flow matching" the exact phrase only alphafold3 AlphaFold3 and AlphaFold 3 over-conditioning, co-folding the two parts next to each other (over-conditioning, over conditioning) and the joined word (cofolding) 10.1038/s41586-024-07487-w, https://doi.org/…, 2210.02747, arXiv:2210.02747 that paper the, of, for … ignored unless the query has nothing else

Other punctuation (:, brackets, slashes) is treated as a word break, so title: diffusion or SE(3) are safe to type.

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text: From the second character on, a dropdown lists matching papers (by title), authors, topics, tags and projects with their paper counts. Use ↑ / ↓ and Enter, or click: a paper opens it; an author, topic, tag or project becomes a filter (and the typed text is cleared). Esc closes the list.

docs.title: Modes, sort, references
docs.text:
Above the results:

  • Exact matches words only. Hybrid (the default) also ranks papers whose title and abstract mean something close to the query, which helps for questions in plain language ("why do co-folding models collapse to one pose"). Meaning ranks by meaning alone. Meaning search needs a one-time embedding of the library in the background (a few minutes); until it is ready, the page says so and shows exact matches.
  • Sort: Relevance (default with a query), Newest added, Year, Title. The sort in Settings applies to browsing without a query.
  • References: also search the cited references that have no PDF in your library (hidden by default; they rank below your own papers).

The query, filters, mode, sort and the references switch are kept in the URL, so a search can be bookmarked or shared. When nothing matches, the page offers to search the references, to search by meaning, or to remove the filters.

The ✦ button next to the box still turns a plain-language request into filters with the AI model.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
The left sidebar provides filters that narrow down the paper list:

Filter How it works Tag Shows papers tagged with the selected tag Topic Shows papers about the selected research topic Project Shows papers belonging to the selected project Person Shows papers authored by or involving the selected person (pick an author in the search suggestions)

Multiple filters can be combined, with or without a search query. Active filters appear as removable chips below the search bar. Tag, topic and venue filters ignore case.

docs.title: Tag Categories
docs.text:
157 tags are seeded on startup:

review, benchmark, dataset, method, theory, negative-result, foundational, highly-cited, sota

algebra, topology, differential-geometry, probability, statistics, optimization, graph-theory, information-theory, and more

docs.title: MCP Server (Claude Desktop)
docs.text: PaperManager ships with an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server at backend/mcp_server.py. This lets Claude Desktop interact with your library directly via natural language.

docs.title: 1 — Locate your Python binary
docs.text:
conda activate papermanager
which python
# e.g. /Users/you/miniconda3/envs/papermanager/bin/python

docs.title: 2 — Configure Claude Desktop
docs.text:
Edit ~/.claude/claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "paperManager": {
      "command": "/path/to/conda/envs/papermanager/bin/python",
      "args": ["/path/to/PaperManager/backend/mcp_server.py"]
    }
  }
}

Replace the paths with your actual paths. Restart Claude Desktop.

docs.title: 3 — Verify
docs.text: Ask Claude: "Can you list my recent papers?" — Claude should call search_papers and return results from your library.

docs.title: Available Tools
docs.text: Tool Description search_papers Search by keyword, tag, topic, project, or person library_lookup Which of up to 200 DOIs / titles are already in the library: one compact line per item (id, projects, citation stub or not), no summaries. Use it before adding cited papers so nothing is added twice get_paper_detail Full paper metadata for one paper chat_with_paper Ask a question about a paper's content add_note Write or update a paper's markdown note get_note Read a paper's note tag_paper_with Add a tag to a paper add_topic Link a research topic to a paper link_person_to_paper Link a person to a paper with a role add_paper_metadata Add a paper by metadata only (no PDF) list_projects List all projects list_project_papers Papers in a specific project add_to_project Add a paper to a project list_tags All tags with paper counts list_topics All topics with paper counts list_people All people get_person_papers Papers associated with a person add_person Create a person node create_project Create a new project upload_pdf Add a paper with its PDF (local path, URL, arXiv id or DOI) find_duplicates Duplicate groups, each with the paper to keep merge_papers Merge duplicates into one paper, nothing lost (dry_run by default) update_paper_metadata Correct title, year, venue, DOI, abstract or the author list regenerate_summary Re-run the AI summary from the stored full text delete_paper Delete a paper with its note, highlights and PDF (needs confirm=true) list_conferences Conference-years the conference explorer has loaded conference_topic Who publishes on a topic at a conference: top universities and companies, area mix, closest papers; conference="all" for every loaded conference with papers per 1,000 per conference and the trend over years conference_institution One institution at a conference: rank, counts, area mix, collaborators, papers conference_search_papers Papers across all loaded conferences by title words (typos tolerated), then by meaning conference_search_author An author across all loaded conferences: papers per conference with their institution on each, possible namesakes

docs.title: Example Interactions
docs.text:
You: add a note to the Attention is All You Need paper saying
     "@Jan is working on a follow-up to this approach"

Claude: [calls add_note] → note saved, MENTIONS relationship
        created in Neo4j for Jan

You: what papers do I have tagged "to-read" about protein folding?

Claude: [calls search_papers with tag="to-read", topic="Protein Folding"]
        → returns matching papers

You: create a project called "NeurIPS 2025 prep" and add all papers
     tagged "important" to it

Claude: [calls create_project, then search_papers + add_to_project
        for each paper]

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
The MCP server and FastAPI backend share the same service and database layers:

flowchart LR
    CD["Claude Desktop"] -->|"MCP protocol"| MCP["mcp_server.py"]
    Browser["Browser"] -->|"HTTP"| FastAPI["FastAPI routers/"]
    MCP --> Tools["tools/*.py"]
    FastAPI --> Routers["routers/*.py"]
    Tools --> DB["db/queries/"]
    Routers --> DB
    Tools --> Services["services/"]
    Routers --> Services
    DB --> Neo4j["Neo4j Aura"]
    Services --> Drive["Google Drive"]
    Services --> AI["Claude / Ollama"]

PDF upload via MCP

upload_pdf(source, project) runs one paper through the full upload pipeline. source is a local PDF path, a PDF URL, an arXiv id or a DOI. Local paths must lie under HOST_IMPORT_ROOT (e.g. /srv/papers), which is mounted read-only into the backend container.

docs.title: Running the MCP Server Standalone
docs.text:
The server can also be run without Claude Desktop for testing:

conda activate papermanager
cd /path/to/PaperManager
python backend/mcp_server.py

This starts the MCP server in stdio mode, ready to accept tool calls.

docs.title: Paper Detail
docs.text: Click any paper card to open the Paper Detail view (/paper/:id). It has four main panels.

docs.title: Metadata & Abstract
docs.text:
The left panel shows:

  • Title, year, DOI, venue
  • Citation count (from Semantic Scholar)
  • Metadata source badge
  • Authors — click an author chip to open their People profile
  • Topics — click a topic chip to filter the library to that topic
  • Abstract (original)
  • AI summary (generated by Claude Opus during upload)

Click Edit to open a modal where you can update any field.

docs.title: PDF Viewer
docs.text:
Available when a PDF was uploaded (not for URL-only papers). The PDF is streamed from Google Drive and rendered inline in the browser.

Tip

For URL-ingested papers you can still attach a PDF later via the Upload PDF button in the metadata panel.

docs.text:
Figures are extracted from the PDF and stored on Google Drive. The figures panel shows:

  • Figure number and page number
  • Caption (generated by Docling, Ollama, or Claude Vision)
  • Click any figure for full-size view
  • Ask about this figure — opens a vision chat powered by Claude; ask anything about the figure image

docs.title: Extracting Figures
docs.text:
Click Extract Figures and choose a caption method:

Method Description Docling Structural PDF parser — fast, no AI cost Ollama Local LLM captions (default) Claude Vision Highest quality; uses Anthropic API

The default method can be set in Settings.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: A Markdown editor is attached to each paper.

docs.title: Special Syntax
docs.text:
Syntax Effect @PersonName Links to a Person node; creates it if not found #TopicName Links to a Topic node; creates it if not found

When you save a note, all @mentions and #topics become graph relationships:

(Note)-[:MENTIONS]->(Person)
(Note)-[:MENTIONS]->(Topic)

This means you can later query "all notes that mention @Jan" or "all papers with notes about #transformers" from the Cypher editor or knowledge chat.

docs.text: Toggle Preview mode to render the note as formatted Markdown.

docs.title: Outgoing References
docs.text:
Papers that this paper cites. Extracted on-demand and shown in a review list before being saved.

Extraction pipeline (tries in order):

  1. Semantic Scholar /references API (requires a DOI or arXiv id), accepted when it is about as complete as the reference list in the text
  2. An LLM over the reference section, in chunks
  3. A deterministic parser over the reference section (also the yardstick for 1 and 2)

Identifier check. Every DOI and arXiv id in a list from 2 or 3 is looked up (doi.org, arXiv) before you see it. Ids that do not exist, or that belong to a different paper than the title says, are removed, so a stub is never linked to the wrong paper; where the parser read an author list as the title, the registered title is used instead. This runs without any AI model and takes a second or two per paper.

Each saved reference creates a Paper stub node (title + DOI), tagged from-references, and linked with a CITES relationship. If you later import the full paper by DOI, the stub is enriched rather than duplicated.

docs.title: Incoming Citations
docs.text: Papers in your library that cite this paper. Maintained automatically as you import papers.

docs.title: Concepts, tour and concept map
docs.text:
Three tools help you understand papers rather than just store them. Concepts and the Tour work on one paper; the concept map works on a whole project.

Tool Where What you get Needs Concepts Paper view → Concepts tab Visual explanations of ideas, marked on the PDF page Claude (subscription or API key) Tour Paper view → Tour tab An overview and 6–12 stops through the PDF Claude Code on a subscription Concept map Projects → a project → Concept map One graph of the key concepts across all papers in the project An OpenAI-compatible model (LITELLM_*)

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
1. Open a paper with a PDF and switch to the Concepts tab.
  2. Click Find concepts. The pages are read in batches; on each page, up to three ideas that a picture explains best are marked.
  3. Click a concept to generate its visualisation, or Generate all for the rest.

Each concept gets one of four kinds of visualisation:

  • Formula: an equation broken into its parts, with what each symbol means
  • Graph: a plot drawn from data points (lines, points or bars)
  • Explanation: a short structured text
  • Animation: a small 2D animation, run in a sandboxed frame

Clicking a mark on the PDF opens its concept, and the other way round. This feature is adapted from Get It. (Apache-2.0).

docs.title: Quick tour
docs.text:
Open the Tour tab and click Make a quick tour. After a minute you get:

  • an overview of what the paper does and why it matters,
  • what to skip on a first read,
  • 6–12 stops, each tied to an exact passage in the PDF, with a short explanation and the concepts it relies on.

Click a stop, or press ← / →, and the PDF scrolls to that passage and highlights it. The tour is saved with the paper; Regenerate tour makes a new one.

Setup

The tour runs Sonnet through Claude Code on a Claude subscription. Set CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN (from claude setup-token) and CLAUDE_CODE_USERS in .env. Without them the button stays disabled; there is no API-key fallback.

docs.title: Concept map
docs.text:
The concept map shows what a set of papers is about and how the ideas connect.

  • Circles are concepts; the colour is the kind (method, model, dataset, task, …) and the size is how many papers discuss it.
  • Papers can be shown too, sized by citations, with their authors optional.
  • Lines are typed relations from the papers: is a, part of, uses, extends, improves on, alternative to, evaluated on and more.
  • Filters narrow the map by author, year, kind and the minimum number of papers per concept. The list beside the graph groups all concepts by kind.

Papers are mapped automatically: every ten minutes, PaperManager maps project papers that have a summary but no concepts yet. Map new papers does it right away; Rebuild all starts over. Set CONCEPT_MAP_AUTO=false to switch the automatic run off.

For each paper the model returns 6–15 concepts with the paper's role for each (introduces, extends, uses, evaluates, critiques or background). It reuses names that already exist in the project, so the same idea from two papers becomes one circle.
